title: Introduction to Reproducible Analysis
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of introduction to reproducible analysis and identify its main inputs, outputs or constraints.
Apply reproducibility and repeatability in a minimal example and state the expected result before checking it.
Test one relevant edge, missing or failure case and describe a limitation of the result.

content.intro: Introduction to Reproducible Analysis is part of Reproducible Research, Reports, and Documentation. Start with reproducibility and repeatability and connect it to the worked example and expected result.
content.why_it_matters: A reproducible analysis records its inputs, code, dependency versions, assumptions, outputs and limitations so another person can rerun it.

content_blocks.title: Why this matters
content_blocks.text: A reproducible analysis records its inputs, code, dependency versions, assumptions, outputs and limitations so another person can rerun it. The example is intentionally small so you can predict its result before checking it in a local R session.

content_blocks.title: Work through it
content_blocks.text: Describe the input files and package versions, then outline how to render the report and verify its output. Change one input or condition at a time, compare the observed result with your prediction, and write down one limitation.

content_blocks.title: R example: Introduction to Reproducible Analysis
content_blocks.code:
# Lesson 173: Introduction to Reproducible Analysis
report_checks <- c("inputs recorded", "method documented", "limit stated")
length(report_checks)
content_blocks.run_instructions: CodeLeaf does not provide an R runtime. This block is an inspectable reference example; execute it in a local R console or a reviewed R-aware environment. Static validation checks file structure, not R semantics.
content_blocks.reset_steps: No example is executed by this CodeLeaf lesson. For a local run, use synthetic data in a temporary working directory, avoid production credentials or destructive writes, and restart a clean R session to clear lesson objects.
content_blocks.limitations: A report should record inputs, software versions, transformation choices and limitations. Verify the snippet and expected output with the supported R and package versions before publishing.

content_blocks.title: Common pitfall
content_blocks.text: Do not treat a syntactically plausible example as proof of correctness. For introduction to reproducible analysis, check the input type, missing/empty cases, output shape, and domain assumptions.

content.task: Apply introduction to reproducible analysis to a small synthetic example. Start with reproducibility and repeatability, predict the result, compare it with a local R run, test one edge or failure case, and document one limitation. For integrations or package-dependent topics, submit a safe verification plan rather than claiming the code ran.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use the reproducibility and repeatability idea in a minimal example or safe design sketch.
State the expected result before running the example.
Verify one relevant boundary, missing-value or failure case.
Record assumptions and one limitation of the result.
content.expected_output: A reproducible introduction to reproducible analysis example or design sketch with the expected result, one checked edge or failure case, and a stated limitation.
hints: Start with “Reproducibility and Repeatability” and identify the input and output before coding.
Inspect the type and shape of the result, then test one ordinary and one boundary input.
Test a boundary, missing, invalid or failure input relevant to this topic.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example without checking its inputs or output shape.
common_mistakes.why: R can coerce types, propagate missing values or simplify results unexpectedly.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect with str(), class(), typeof(), length() or dim() and add a direct check.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a demonstration as proof that every edge case works.
common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing values, dependencies and version differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Test a normal case and a boundary/failure case in a clean local R session.

common_mistakes.why: The conclusion depends on data provenance, transformations and assumptions.
common_mistakes.fix: Record input source, cleaning choices and known limitations beside the result.
